whatTheyArgued: Verified snip, Principles of Judicial Proof (1913), Part II intro no. 163 (adapted from his Treatise on Evidence, 1905, I section 478): any assertion offered as the basis of an inference that the thing asserted happened is testimony, in court or not; testimony has three necessary stages, Perception, Recollection, Communication; and the canons for weighing a witness correspond to those three. Separately, in his Treatise on Evidence section 1367 he called cross-examination the greatest legal engine for discovering truth (quoted in legal literature; I did not open the Treatise). He also built the chart method for mapping evidence and inferences (Goodwin; Twining).

scholarship.ref: Search results on Wigmore: cross-examination quotation (Evidence 1367), Twining 'Theories of Evidence: Bentham and Wigmore' (1985), and the chart method (listing only; pages not opened)
scholarship.supports: chart method as his answer to a missing science of proof; cross-examination as his famous tool
scholarship.disputes: Twining and others treat Wigmore's chart method as demanding and rarely used in practice; not verified here

ourUse: testimony.js asks a small model one binary question twice (does the passage say the claim is true; then the same for a sibling-swapped twin, a name swapped for another name on the page) and derives the verdict mechanically from the pair; the model is never trusted on its own word.

bends.ours: organ header and compendium: Wigmore 'charted testimony by asking the witness twice and reading the verdict from the pair'; 'cross-examination as asking the witness more than once'.
bends.theirs: Nothing in the verified passage, nor in his famous cross-examination claim, describes asking twice or a swapped twin; the swap-control is the project's own perturbation test.

bends.ours: The snip quoted at the top is the Perception/Recollection/Communication analysis, but testimony.js does not model those stages; grep finds them only in the header quote.
bends.theirs: His point is that belief in testimony must be assessed at each of the three stages; we test one thing, whether a page's bytes state a sentence.

bends.ours: The 'witness' is a small language model reading a passage.
bends.theirs: A witness is a person with perception and memory who can be cross-examined; a model reading a page has none of the three stages, and the page is the testimony, not the model.

bends.ours: header: 'My teaching advocates for the meticulous application of these principles...' under 'Wigmore speaks'.
bends.theirs: A generated first-person paragraph set in his voice; not his words.

bends.ours: compendium source: 'The Science of Judicial Proof (1913; 3rd ed. 1937)', pdStatus fair-use.
bends.theirs: The verified snip is the 1913 Principles of Judicial Proof (public domain). The Science of Judicial Proof is the retitled 1937 edition; the 1913 date does not fit that title. Standing here is verified through the 1913 text only.
